### Quarto websites & collaborative coding (W5)

*What we did:* we didn't branch our repository, as we thought it was best to avoid any merging issues in the long game. It turned out to be a good decision, as we didn't have too many different documents to work on so it was fine in the end. For a bigger, more detailed analysis this would not have worked out.
In terms of the website, only one person was responsible for the web layout. We relied on the sketch offered on the course git and followed that.

*What worked well:*

*What was hard:* since multiple people worked on the same script, there was the fear of maybe deleting each others progress. we tried to avoid this by working in different sections, so everyone would focus on their individual question.

### R packages (W6)

*What we did:* we relied on the basic r packages, like **tidyverse** and **ggplot** for visualization. We also had to rely on **readxl** since the data set we were wokring with did not come from a package or so, but was an existing Exel sheet. 

*What worked well:* Installing them

*What was hard:* The big question was how we would ensure reproduceability, as one needs all the packages we used to run our code. We solved this by setting it up in the "Set-up.R" file, to make sure that any packages that might be missing on your devise, will be installed previous to any further analysis steps. 
We also decided against creating our own package, as we didn't rely on many functions and mostly coded working directly with the data. We realized too late that we could have relied on the natural structure of packages, which could have saved as some time looking back. In the end we didn't want to change the entire repository structure, out of fear of messing something up.

### Initial data analysis & data cleaning (W7)

*What we did:* We first all took a look at the raw data, and tried to understand what the variables represent. The first thing we notices, what that for some variables (e.g. par_1_rr for CZ) we had a lot of missing values, which were not coded as such. We also realzied that we were working with categorized variables, and discussed how to handle this best.

*What worked well:* clearing out the NAs?

*What was hard:* Deciding which variables were relevant for our analysis, it was difficult to limit the scope of the analysis. It didn't make sense to check out all countries, because some had a lot of NAs, but it would also be statistically incorrect to completly ignore them. We also had to discuss how deal with the NAs, and what types of parental leave we wanted to focus on because we were looking at multiple categories for different types of parental leave.

## Workflow & collaboration

*How did we divide work across group members?* Each member focused on one question. Everybody worked from the main branch. We thought this would be the easiest way to later gather all the information.

*What branching or Git workflow did we actually use — and did it match the proposal?*

*What would we change about how we coordinated?* Splitting up into branches might have been better, as sometimes two people were working on the same script, which could have caused some merging issues. If we had relied on branches, we could have done more work individually without being afraid to mess with somebody elses work.
